sections.title: How does the PSIG to PSIA conversion calculator work?
sections.html:
The PSIG to PSIA conversion calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports pressure in pounds per square inch absolute in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the pressure in pounds per square inch gauge.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in pounds per square inch gauge. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.

Both boxes accept a value, so it does not matter which one you start from. Type into the box you already know — the number in the other box is rewritten as soon as you press Calculate, and the unit chips beside them let you move to a third and fourth unit without leaving the page.

sections.title: The formula behind the PSIG to PSIA conversion calculator
sections.html:
Spelled out as an equation, 1 psig = 15.6959 psi. The scales are not proportional, so the offset matters too: 0 psig = 14.6959 psi. Everything else on this page follows from that one line.

This is a conversion rather than a calculation. Pressure in pounds per square inch absolute and pressure in pounds per square inch gauge describe the same quantity, so the arithmetic underneath is a simple identity: whatever you type in one box is converted to a common base unit, and the other box is rendered from that base in its own unit.

That is why changing the unit chip does not change the underlying value, only the way it is written — and why you can enter a figure in either box and read the answer from the other.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in pounds per square inch, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Pressure, opening in pounds per square inch gauge
  • Pressure, opening in pounds per square inch

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The PSIG to PSIA conversion calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a product listing against the measurements you work with
  • Filling in a form that asks for imperial or metric values
  • Reading a recipe written in units you do not use
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the pressure in pounds per square inch gauge — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the PSIG to PSIA conversion calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns pressure in pounds per square inch absolute, derived from the pressure in pounds per square inch gauge. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the PSIG to PSIA conversion calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the pressure in pounds per square inch gauge, which is 1 field in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter pressure in pounds per square inch gauge in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Pressure in pounds per square inch gauge opens in pounds per square inch gauge and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the PSIG to PSIA conversion calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
